content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review_assessment:_thoroughness_in_paper: I made a quick assessment of this paper.
content.review:
This paper proposes a method for performing data augmentation using self-supervision and self-distillation. One of the main problems of data augmentation is that the data transformations have to be tunned for each dataset. E.g., in MNIST a "9" rotated 180 degrees would be a "6". This paper proposes a method using self-supervision (i.e., predict the rotation and color channel flips). Instead of having a multitask loss (i.e., one loss for predicting the object class and another for the self-supervision transformation), this paper proposes to frame the problem as a single classification problem where the new label is obtained by the permutation of object labels and self-supervised ones.

The method is tested in 3 scenarios: image classification, few-shot image classification, and imbalanced data image classification. In the first case, the proposed method is compared with performing data augmentation (without hyperparameter tunning in the best setting, I assume it is just the same transformations used for the self-supervised case) and with the multi-task setting (where the self-supervised and object classification tasks are in different losses). The results show that DA performs worse than the baseline (Obviously because the parameters used does not make sense) and the same for multitask learning. Then several ablation studies are done and also experiments on a few-shot and imbalanced classification.

Main problem:

The evaluation is not fair. In the case of image classification, the method should be compared to standard data augmentation with correct parameters and with SOTA methods of automatic data augmentation which do not require tunning the DA parameters. It should be compared at leat with:
 - AutoAugment: Learning Augmentation Policies from Data
 - Fast AutoAugment
 - Adversarial Learning of General Transformations for Data Augmentation
 - DADA: Deep Adversarial Data Augmentation for Extremely Low Data Regime Classification
 - TANDA: Learning to Compose Domain-Specific Transformations for Data Augmentation
 
The evaluation for few-shot and imbalanced is compared with other methods of the literature. However, no-one of these methods use data augmentation and then the comparison is not relevant.

content.comment: Have you used the pretrained ResNet18 model on ImageNet and then finetune on TinyImageNet? I have tried to train the TinyImageNet using ResNet18 from scratch, however, the performance is very low. So can you share more training details on the training settings, especially for TinyImageNet on ResNet18.
content.title: Training ResNet18 on TinyImageNet

replying_to: Replying to Training ResNet18 on TinyImageNet

content.comment:
All reported models in our paper were trained from scratch (i.e., we do not use ImageNet pre-training). We use PyTorch with torchvision in our experiments and the training details for TinyImageNet are as follows (see Section 3.1):

- We use ResNet18 (in torchvision.models module).
- We use SGD (in torch.optim) with a batch size of 128, weight decay of 10^-4 and momentum of 0.9.
- We set the initial learning rate by 0.1 and decay the learning rate by a factor 0.1 at 40k and 60k iterations. The total number of training iterations is 80k.
- We also use the conventional data augmentation techniques, random cropping (i.e., RandomResizedCrop(224)) and horizontal flipping (i.e., RandomHorizontalFlip()), which are implemented in “torchvision.transforms” module.

Just after the paper decision, we plan to release our code and you can check the full details on how we implement the training procedure.

Thanks for your interest in our paper !

content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review:
To solve the distributional discrepancy when performing data augmentation, this paper proposes to learn the joint distribution of the original and self-supervised labels of augmented examples. The idea is easy to understand and implement. The authors then perform an empirical study on a standard setting (e.g. CIFAR 10/100) and a limited data setting (e.g. few-shot). 


I have some concerns as follows:

1. The proposed method is not scalable. For a classification task with 1000 classes and 10 rotations, there will be 10000 labels to predict. 
2. AutoAugment (https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.09501) can learn a transform function to avoid the distributional discrepancy, but the authors did not compare theirs with this strong baseline. 
3. The experiments done on MIT-67 seems not meaningful to me, as the dataset is old and small (published in 2009).

content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I carefully checked the derivations and theory.
content.review:
This paper proposes to use data-augmentation as self-supervision, applied as a regularizer in fully supervised classification settings in order to improve the generalization accuracy of the classifier. It uses a joint (label x augmentation) prediction space, rather than a factorized space of labels and augmentations in distinct prediction branches (multi-task setting). The author argues that this alleviates the requirement of invariance w.r.t. the transformation for the primary classifier and allows to use more diverse augmentations. The author tests this hypothesis on various classification datasets (including few-shot and fine-grained), and also evaluates the approach with test-time augmentation - proposing a knowledge distillation method to alleviate its cost. The author show improved accuracies in these settings w.r.t. simple data-augmentation (DA) or multi-task (MT) baselines.

I am unsure about the justification of the method’s advantage w.r.t. the baseline and MT. I have the impression that the performance improvements w.r.t. MT could be explained by the added capacity. Barring futher experimental validation that this is not the case, I find the contributions of the paper to be minor. I will detail these points hereunder.

* Method *
1. The features learned by MT are not invariant by the transformations (otherwise the auxiliary classifier could not predict the transformation). The primary classifier in MT could behave in a similar way as the SDA method by aggregating features from a joint (label x augmentation) space, acting as a projection on the label subspace. Therefore, I do not see in MT the core limitation that SDA claims to address (enforcing extraneous invariance of the classifier).
2. I see the joint classifier in SDA as the bulk of the novelty: the test-time augmentation experiments and teacher/student models to relieve the costs of these test-time augmentations are good to have but do not seem novel, and their applicability is not restricted to the SDA approach.

* Experiments *
3. It is my understanding that SDA uses FxN(M-1) more parameters in the classifier than the baseline and than MT (F: number of features). This provides more parameters for the network to absorb the data augmentations, and to perform better for the primary classification task. This added capacity could explain the accuracy gains with respect to MT and to the baseline.
For a fair comparison, a similar capacity should be added to the baseline, to DA and to MT.
For the baseline, this could be done e.g. by using a large F x N x M classifier, and using a pooling over the M dimension.
For DA, this could be done by using a large F x N x M classifier, and selecting the FxN slice that corresponds to the augmentation used (just as was done for SDA, but without the data-augmentation loss term in eq. 2).
For MT, this could be done by adding an additional fully-connected layer before the two heads.

* Minor *

content.title: Response for All Reviewers
content.comment:
We thank all reviewers for helpful and constructive comments on our paper. We address the comments one by one as below.

- Comparison with SOTA augmentation methods (R1, R3)
The major concern of reviewers (R1, R3) is that there is no comparison with SOTA augmentation techniques such as AutoAugment. We want to remark that our paper proposes an orthogonal direction to the existing data augmentation methods. This is because we use semantically-sensitive transformations while the data augmentation methods should use semantically-invariant transformations. For example, AutoAugment uses Rotation of degree in [-30°,30°] for preserving input’s semantic however we use 90°, 180°, 270° rotated images for modifying the semantic. Therefore, the transformations for ours and data augmentation methods are mutually exclusive. Due to this, we think that data augmentation is a complementer, not a competitor. Moreover, we expect that our method can be well-combined with the advanced augmentation methods such as AutoAugment.

- Fairness on few-shot and imbalance experiments (R1)
We think that proving wide applicability is important because applying a method into different tasks is not always straightforward. For example, when we train ProtoNet [1] with the AutoAugment policy on few-shot learning tasks, we cannot obtain an accuracy gain. Moreover, as we mentioned above, any additional data augmentation techniques are not our competitors, and they can improve both ours and the baselines. Thus we think that our evaluation is valid, and it shows that the proposed method can be used widely.

- Verification (R2)
As R2 mentioned, the intermediate features might be not invariant to the transformations. However, the constraint (w_ij=u_i+v_j) forces independence between features related to self-supervised and original tasks on the embedding space. Since the two features are closely related, it is hard to decompose them. Therefore, learning features with the constraint is harder than that without the constraint. The difficulty causes degradation on the accuracy, as reported in our paper.

- The novelty of aggregation & self-distillation schemes (R2)
Our aggregation scheme acts as an ensemble of multiple models, thus it is quite different from other aggregation schemes like ten-crop. Therefore, self-distillation performs well because it utilizes the aggregation. We think that these methods are well-combined with the proposed framework, so we believe that they are also valuable in this paper as well.

- Efficiency & Scalability (R2, R3)
We want to note that the number of additional parameters is negligible compared to that of the body of neural networks. For example, ResNet32 with 10 classes has 464,154 parameters, and ResNet32 with 40 classes uses 466,104. It means that the joint label classifier increases only 0.4% parameters.

For scalability, one can control the type of self-supervision and the number of self-supervised labels for her purpose. Therefore, for a dataset of a large number of labels, one might choose 2~4 self-supervised labels such as rotation. As reported in our paper, we think such a small number of self-supervised labels is enough to provide meaningful improvements. During this rebuttal period, we run an experiment on ImageNet with 1,000 classes and 128 samples per class (we reduce the number of samples as any data augmentation method is more meaningful to test under less-data regimes). In this experiment, the baseline and SDA+AG (with 4 self-supervised rotations) achieve 47.69% and 52.26% in their accuracy, respectively. The results show that the scalability of our method with respect to the number of classes.

[1] Jake Snell et al., Prototypical Networks for Few-shot Learning
